name: Database Server Hunt
author: Data Security Team
prerequisites: Database audit logging enabled (general query log
DBA read-only access to system tables and audit logs
Network access logs for database ports (1433
required_tools: SQL Server Audit / MySQL Enterprise Audit / pgAudit
SolarWinds DPA or equivalent query analysis tool

hunt_actions.title: Unauthorized Access and Privilege Escalation
actions: Enumerate database accounts with excessive privileges (SQL Server): `SELECT p.name, p.type_desc, p.is_disabled, r.name AS role_name FROM sys.database_principals p LEFT JOIN sys.database_role_members rm ON p.principal_id = rm.member_principal_id LEFT JOIN sys.database_principals r ON rm.role_principal_id = r.principal_id WHERE r.name IN ('db_owner','sysadmin','securityadmin') ORDER BY p.name;` — compare against approved DBA list.

Detect database accounts created outside change windows: MySQL: `SELECT user, host, password_last_changed, account_locked FROM mysql.user ORDER BY password_last_changed DESC LIMIT 20;` SQL Server: `SELECT name, create_date, modify_date, type_desc FROM sys.server_principals WHERE type IN ('S','U') ORDER BY create_date DESC;` — any account created without a corresponding change ticket is a finding.

Hunt for xp_cmdshell execution in SQL Server (OS command execution): `SELECT event_time, server_principal_name, database_name, statement FROM sys.fn_get_audit_file('/var/opt/mssql/audit/*.sqlaudit', DEFAULT, DEFAULT) WHERE statement LIKE '%xp_cmdshell%' ORDER BY event_time DESC;` — xp_cmdshell should be disabled; any execution indicates active exploitation or misconfiguration.

Identify UDF or stored procedure abuse for privilege escalation: MySQL: `SELECT routine_name, routine_schema, security_type, definer FROM information_schema.routines WHERE security_type='DEFINER' AND definer LIKE 'root%' ORDER BY last_altered DESC;` — stored procedures running as root/sa with user-controllable inputs are SQL injection risks.

hunt_actions.title: Data Exfiltration Detection
actions: Detect bulk SELECT operations returning large datasets: SQL Server Audit or pgAudit: `SELECT user_name, client_hostname, COUNT(*) as query_count, SUM(rows_affected) as total_rows FROM database_audit_log WHERE action='SELECT' AND timestamp > NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days' GROUP BY user_name, client_hostname HAVING total_rows > 100000 ORDER BY total_rows DESC;` — users or service accounts pulling > 100,000 rows outside normal application behavior are high-priority.

Hunt for SELECT INTO OUTFILE or mysqldump usage (MySQL data export): `grep -E 'SELECT.+INTO OUTFILE|mysqldump|mysqlpump|mydumper' /var/log/mysql/mysql-general.log | grep -v '127.0.0.1' | awk '{print $1, $2, $NF}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20` — all data export operations should be authorized and logged.

Identify database linked server / dblink queries to unknown hosts: SQL Server: `SELECT name, provider, data_source, is_linked FROM sys.servers WHERE is_linked=1;` PostgreSQL: `SELECT srvname, srvoptions FROM pg_foreign_server;` — linked servers to unknown external hosts may be used for data exfiltration via SQL queries.

Detect database files or backup dumps created recently: `find /var/lib/mysql /var/lib/postgresql /opt/mssql/data -name '*.bak' -o -name '*.dump' -o -name '*.sql' -o -name '*.tar.gz' -newer /etc/passwd | ls -lh 2>/dev/null | sort -k5 -rn` — unauthorized database dumps indicate active data theft; also: `SELECT name, physical_name, state_desc, create_date FROM sys.master_files ORDER BY create_date DESC;` (SQL Server).

hunt_actions.title: Database Configuration and Persistence Checks
actions: Check for database-level triggers used for persistence: SQL Server: `SELECT t.name, o.name AS parent_table, t.is_disabled, m.definition FROM sys.triggers t JOIN sys.objects o ON t.parent_id=o.object_id JOIN sys.sql_modules m ON t.object_id=m.object_id ORDER BY t.modify_date DESC;` MySQL: `SELECT TRIGGER_SCHEMA, TRIGGER_NAME, EVENT_OBJECT_TABLE, ACTION_STATEMENT FROM information_schema.triggers ORDER BY LAST_ALTERED DESC LIMIT 20;`

Verify SQL Server audit is enabled and intact: `SELECT name, audit_file_path, status_desc, max_file_size FROM sys.server_audits;` and `SELECT * FROM sys.server_audit_specifications; SELECT * FROM sys.database_audit_specifications;` — verify audit covers LOGIN, LOGOUT, OBJECT_ACCESS, SCHEMA_OBJECT_ACCESS, and EXECUTE actions; any gaps indicate potential tampering.

Hunt for unauthorized network connections to database ports: `ss -tnp | grep -E ':1433|:3306|:5432|:1521|:27017'` and `netstat -an | grep ESTABLISHED | grep -E '1433|3306|5432|1521'` — compare active connection source IPs against approved application servers and DBA workstations list; any unexpected source is a finding.

questions: Is database-level auditing enabled on all production database servers, capturing at minimum authentication events, privilege use, DDL changes, and bulk data access operations?
Are database audit logs forwarded to an independent SIEM or immutable log store that is inaccessible to database administrators, ensuring audit log integrity?

Is the principle of least privilege enforced for all database accounts, with application service accounts restricted to only the schemas and operations required by the application (no db_owner or DBA-level roles)?
Are all database servers restricted to accept connections only from approved application server IP ranges via network access controls (firewall rules, security groups, or host-based ACLs)?

Is xp_cmdshell disabled on all SQL Server instances (verify with `SELECT value_in_use FROM sys.configurations WHERE name='xp_cmdshell'`), and are all other extended stored procedures that enable OS interaction audited?

Are database backup files encrypted at rest and stored in a location inaccessible to the database service account, and is access to backup files subject to the same access controls as production data?

Are database credentials for application service accounts stored in a secrets management system (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault) with automatic rotation, rather than in application configuration files?

Is a Database Activity Monitoring (DAM) solution deployed on all databases containing Personally Identifiable Information (PII), Protected Health Information (PHI), or financial data, as required by applicable regulatory frameworks?
